title: Authority in Capernaum (Mark 1:21–28)
hook: in the synagogue he teaches with authority, and an unclean spirit shrieks
tomorrow: a mother-in-law and a whole town

segments.voice: Yesterday: immediately, Mark's favorite word, and four fishermen dropping their nets. Your line was leave the nets. What did you do right away? Day one hundred sixty.

Saturday morning in a fishing town called Capernaum, on the north shore of the lake. It's the Sabbath, and the town is at the synagogue. A visiting teacher is invited to speak, which was normal. What isn't normal is how he speaks. People lean in. Something in his voice is different from anything they've heard. And then, in the middle of it, a scream. A man in the congregation, a man with what Mark calls an unclean spirit, shrieking at the teacher, as if something inside him knows exactly who this is and is terrified. Everyone freezes. Today: what happened next, and the word the whole town was talking about by lunchtime.
screen: `SABBATH IN CAPERNAUM.` → `THE WAY HE SPEAKS.` → `A SCREAM IN THE SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: Authority in Capernaum. First, the teaching. Mark says, in the King James Bible: "And they were astonished at his doctrine: for he taught them as one that had authority, and not as the scribes." The scribes were careful teachers, and good ones often taught by citing earlier teachers: this rabbi said, that sage said. Jesus seems to speak directly. The Greek for authority is exousia. It's built from ex, out of, and a word for being. Authority that comes out of who you are, not from a title or a footnote. Mark never tells us what Jesus taught that morning. Just how it landed. Then the scream. "Let us alone; what have we to do with thee, thou Jesus of Nazareth? art thou come to destroy us? I know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God." Here's the odd thing: in Mark, the spirits are the first to recognize who Jesus is, before the disciples, before the crowds. And Jesus doesn't want their announcement. "Hold thy peace, and come out of him." Hold thy peace is gentle in English. The Greek is blunt: be muzzled. Be quiet. Then: come out. The man convulses, the spirit cries out, and it's gone. And the town talks about one thing: what is this? A new teaching, with authority, and even the unclean spirits obey him. Christians read these stories in different ways. Many understand them as real encounters with spiritual evil. Many also hear in them every voice that holds a person captive and won't let go. Mark's point is the same either way: the same authority that teaches also frees. One word, and the man got his life back.
screen: `NOT AS THE SCRIBES.` · `EXOUSIA — OUT OF WHO HE IS.` · `THE SPIRITS KNOW HIM FIRST.` · `BE MUZZLED. COME OUT.` · then, large: `HOLD THY PEACE, AND COME OUT OF HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Most of us carry a voice inside that doesn't help. The one that says you're not enough, you'll fail, nobody wants you here. Listen for it gently. Don't argue with it. Just notice what it says and how old it sounds. If the voice is heavy or frightening, that's something to share with someone you trust or a professional, not to carry alone. If you pray, you can bring it to God and say the words of the story: be quiet, come out. If you don't, you can simply set it down for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Authority in Capernaum. Exousia: authority that comes out of who he is. It teaches, and it frees.
Your line: be quiet, come out. Today, when a voice in you starts tearing you down, notice it, and don't let it run the room. Day one hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Many Christians read Mark's healing and deliverance stories as signs of Jesus's authority over evil; churches differ in how they understand unclean spirits today, and many pray for freedom from whatever binds a person.

fork.setup: you're teaching in the synagogue. a man shrieks: I know who you are, the Holy One of God! what do you do?
options: thank him for saying who you are.
tell the spirit to be quiet and come out.
fork.reveal: "hold thy peace, and come out of him." the spirit is silenced, the man is freed, and the town asks: what is this?

original.note: Greek: authority, power to act — from ex, out of, and a word for being.

trapdoor: what you thought: authority means being in charge.
what it means: a word that teaches and frees, coming out of who Jesus is, not from a title.
what a scholar hears: exousia; and phimōthēti, be muzzled (1:25). Mark's 'messianic secret': Jesus repeatedly silences those who name him.

notes: Scribes and teaching by citing earlier authorities: a common explanation, partly based on later rabbinic practice; confirm the phrasing avoids caricature ('careful teachers, and good ones').
Etymology of exousia (ex + ousia/einai) is a common homiletic gloss; confirm.

Care: unclean spirits presented with two Christian readings, without ranking; practice includes a pointer to trusted people/professionals for heavy or frightening inner voices, to avoid implying mental illness is demonic. Please check.
